source.title: The Quenching-Activation Behavior of the Gradient Descent Dynamics for Two-layer Neural Network Models
source.authors: Chao Ma; Lei Wu; E. Weinan

record.tranche_reason: Sweeps network width and reports test error and path norm under gradient descent, testing width-related generalization behavior with synthetic regression targets rather than the datasets and setup in V2.
record.gate_note: Results use made-up regression targets drawn from Barron-function examples. The text explicitly reports a test-error peak near m=n and no peak near m=n/(d+1); cited findings from other work are not rows.
record.test_reason: The study measures held-out regression error while widening one-hidden-layer ReLU networks trained by unregularized GD to training error below 10^-5. These results test V2 in a new setting of synthetic target functions.
record.authors_conclusion: The record accurately summarizes Section 5 but omits the main conclusions. Under conventional scaling, GD transitions from sparse, NN-like quenching–activation behavior to RF-like behavior as width grows, and generalization can deteriorate. Mean-field scaling produces more stable width dependence, though performance is not always better. The authors propose quenching–activation as a mechanism of implicit regularization.
record.recipe_differences: Two-layer ReLU networks trained by gradient descent on synthetic regression targets; width sweeps and test error/path norm measurements rather than the specified MNIST and downsampled CIFAR-10 experiment.
record.method_sensitivity: Network width and scaling regime; the paper reports different generalization behavior for conventional and mean-field scaling.

fits_no_version.finding: Path norm increases alongside test error between approximately n/(d+1) and n and also peaks near n.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Path norm indicates generalization performance in these synthetic two-layer regression experiments.

record.problems: The experiments use made-up regression targets rather than natural data. The width-sweep values are presented in figures without exact numerical values in the text, and the authors describe the transition behavior as subjective or fuzzy in related experiments.
record.rows_left_out: No qualifying results left out. Other reported experiments concern training dynamics, target-function fit, or scaling behavior without directly measuring a V2 width-versus-test-error outcome.

untested.parts: Random-label fitting, natural-label accuracy, and chance performance on held-out random labels.

MNIST and downsampled CIFAR-10 classification; exact zero training error and an empirically located minimum fitting width. The one-hidden-layer ReLU architecture and absence of explicit regularization are tested.
Convolutional versus fully connected image classifiers and local connectivity.
Adaptive optimizers versus SGD under limited or broader tuning.
Batch-size comparisons under fixed epoch budgets and recipe adaptations.
Magnitude-aware sharpness, generalization-gap rankings, and comparisons with alternative measures.
Removing memorized examples versus equally many random examples.

missing.what: Mean-field versus conventional width sweeps for both targets: mean-field test error changes more smoothly and shows almost no deterioration even at high width. Record separate target and scaling conditions; the claim that no qualifying results were omitted is incorrect.
missing.locator: Section 6, Figure 18, left panel for each target

record.verdict_notes: A peak near m=n alone does not contradict V2; the explicit increase across already nearly fitted widths supplies the challenge. Exact curve values and post-peak trends cannot be reliably recovered from the supplied figure text. The discussion's statement that implicit regularization allows the norm to grow out of control appears to contain a missing negation, given its following statement that the gap is controlled.

versions.untested_parts: Random-label memorization and natural-label generalization coexistence.
MNIST and downsampled CIFAR-10; the specified one-hidden-layer ReLU setup and explicit comparison to the width needed for zero training error.
Convolutional versus fully connected architecture comparisons on images.
Adaptive optimizers compared with SGD or momentum under different tuning and regularization recipes.
Large versus small batch training under fixed epoch budgets and recipe adaptations.
Magnitude-aware sharpness and comparisons with norm- and margin-based measures.
Removing memorized training examples and measuring the effect on test accuracy.

rows.subject: GD solutions for the single neuron target function f1*
rows.stage_stated: trained with GD; stopped when training error is smaller than 10^-5
rows.operation_detail: Varied the number of neurons and measured test error.
rows.value: figure only; text says a peak occurs around m=n
rows.note: The paper says it does not observe a peak around m=n/(d+1), but does observe one around m=n.
rows.check: The width sweep is not uniformly reversed: test error increases dramatically from approximately n/(d+1) to n and peaks near n. Split the rising and post-peak ranges before assigning directional states. The nominal parameter-count threshold is not an empirically established minimum width for fitting. Baseline should identify narrower networks in the sweep; learning rate is 0.001.
